newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Austria holds emergency debate on Kurd murders.
newsitem.headline: Austria holds emergency debate on Kurd murders.

text.p: Austria's parliament held an emergency debate on Tuesday to enable opposition parties to press the government to respond to allegations it colluded in the flight of suspected Iranian assassins in July 1989.

The opposition Liberal Forum tabled 60 questions to Foreign Minister and conservative People's Party leader Wolfgang Schuessel relating to the murder in Vienna of Iranian Kurdish leader Abdorrahman Qasemlu and two other activists.

The Liberal Forum, with the far-right Freedom Party and leftist Greens, is demanding an independent inquiry into whether the government bowed to pressure from Iran and knowingly allowed three suspected killers to return home.

"Today's extraordinary session provides a chance to restore the credibility of Austrian politics. It's a question of political honesty and whether the principles of government are being sacrificed to political expediency," Liberal Forum leader Heide Schmidt said.

Schuessel, whose party has ruled in coalition with the dominant Social Democrats for more than a decade, defended the actions of ministers at the time but conceded the events were "not a glorious chapter".
Civil servants at the foreign, interior and justice ministries are compiling reports on the case but the government has so far rejected calls for an independent inquiry.
Schuessel promised to make the reports public. "We want to clear this up," he told deputies.

Pressure has been growing since April when a German court linked the 1992 slaying of a group of Kurdish dissidents in Berlin with the Vienna murders. In a verdict that sparked a diplomatic row, it accused Tehran of ordering the Berlin killings.
"The red thread tying the events in Vienna and Berlin is there for all to see," the court said in its judgement.

Whereas German authorities sought to bring the perpetrators to justice, Austrian media and some diplomats have alleged their government allowed suspects to go free and even escorted one to Vienna airport in an official motorcade.
Warrants for their arrest were only issued when they were safely outside Austria.
"The Kurds are dead, the suspects are in Iran and that's the end of it," one justice ministry official was quoted as saying in 1992.

Now the matter is threatening to engulf senior politicians past and present, including President Thomas Klestil, who has yet to decide whether he will stand for reelection in 1998, and former foreign minister Alois Mock. Klestil was state secretary in the foreign ministry at the time of the killings.

Former Iranian president Abolhassan Bani-Sadr told a news conference in Vienna last month that Austria allowed itself to be blackmailed by Iran with threats to leak details of an arms scandal involving Austrian firm Noricum in the 1980s.

The Liberal Forum demanded information from Schuessel on the extent of contacts between Austria and Iran in the months after the murders and urged the government to release the minutes of cabinet meetings at the time.

"Do you see any link between the escape of the Kurds' killers in 1989 and the good relationship between Austria and Iran, which has been characterised more by building up economic ties than discussing human rights?" the Liberal Forum said in a question tabled during the debate, which was likely to last into the night.
